Skip serializing bulk edits when debug logging is off (#341765)

Every bulk edit serializes its full edit list with `JSON.stringify`,
even when debug logging is off. Each `BulkEdit._perform*Edits` call did:

```ts
this._logService.debug('_performTextEdits', JSON.stringify(edits));
```

The string is built before `debug()` checks the log level, so it is
built and then thrown away at the default `Info` level. For Search
**Replace All** that is one stringify of every match on the UI thread.
On 10k matches, it was the largest JS self-time entry in the profile.

This PR moves the four call sites into a `_logEdits` helper that only
serializes when `canLog(getLevel(), LogLevel.Debug)` is true. `canLog`
also handles `LogLevel.Off`. Log output is unchanged when debug logging
is on.

## Measurements

The benchmark ran `BulkEditService.apply` with real `TextModel`s and
`ModelService`. Only the I/O and UI services were stubbed. Each Replace
All was 10k `foo`→`bar` edits. Before and after were built from `main`
(02001a6b31e) and this branch as identical bundles on both machines.
Each process ran 10 warmup applies, then 50 measured ones. Before and
after alternated each round, with 15 rounds per side.

**Instructions per apply** (hardware counter, startup and warmup
subtracted by differencing 0 vs 50 iterations):

| Scenario | Linux, EPYC 9575F VM (`perf`, `instructions:u`) | macOS,
Apple M3 (`time -l`) |
|---|---|---|
| 100 files × 100 matches | 350.3M → 256.7M (**−26.7%**, 95% CI [−26.8,
−26.7]) | 348.7M → 259.7M (**−25.5%**, [−26.4, −25.5]) |
| 1000 files × 10 matches | 416.4M → 314.4M (**−24.5%**, [−24.5, −24.5])
| 413.2M → 314.8M (**−23.8%**, [−24.0, −23.7]) |

**Wall-clock per apply** (per-process median):

| Scenario | Linux (pinned to 1 core) | macOS |
|---|---|---|
| 100 × 100 | 41.6 → 32.4 ms (**−22.1%**, [−26.1, −19.4]) | 16.8 → 12.4
ms (**−26.2%**, [−28.6, −25.2]) |
| 1000 × 10 | 61.1 → 54.0 ms (**−11.7%**, [−15.3, −7.5]) | 20.0 → 15.7
ms (**−21.2%**, [−23.0, −20.0]) |

In all eight comparisons, every after run beat every before run.
Mann–Whitney p ≤ 4e-05; the confidence intervals are bootstrap 95%. In
CPU profiles, self time in `_performTextEdits` dropped from 17–23% to
about 0% on both machines. V8 attributes the `JSON.stringify` built-in
to its caller, so that is where the stringify cost showed up.

These numbers cover only the bulk-edit step of Replace All, not the full
end-to-end operation.

## How to test

- Search for a common token across a workspace, then **Replace All**:
the edits apply and the files save as before.
- With the default log level (Info), the Window log has no
`_performTextEdits` line after Replace All.
- Launched with `--log debug`, Replace All still writes the `[debug]
_performTextEdits [...]` line with every edit serialized (6 of 6 in a
3-file test) to the Window log.
- `npm run typecheck-client` is clean. `scripts/test.sh --grep
"BulkEdit|BulkFileEdits|BulkCellEdits|MainThreadEditors|MainThreadBulkEdits"`
passes.

## Summary
- Accept video/audio as well as image clipboard files; preserve native
names, MIME types, and bytes through existing file/snippet
infrastructure.
- Consume native context-menu clipboard payloads without rereading the
clipboard and report unsupported file-only formats explicitly.
- Fix the webview host-menu focus race: restore the last connected
focused input synchronously before native clipboard commands, without
overriding an already focused input. Update the shell CSP hash.

Companion clipboard strategy:
https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-packages/pull/363. Media support
compiles against published editor types; complete context-menu behavior
requires that package change to be published and adopted. Local
file-linked development dependencies are deliberately excluded from this
PR.

## Validation
- 10 focused Markdown media-paste extension tests and three native-media
classification tests passed.
- Three targeted webview shell tests passed, covering native command
focus, disconnected/existing inputs, and CSP consistency.
- Renderer type-check, extension compilation, webview bundle build, and
targeted ESLint passed.
- Actual Code OSS automated with dbgjs/CDP: keyboard image/video paste
and actual context-menu Paste clicks insert correct image/video markup.
The native command receives the editable Clipboard target rather than
BODY; the proxy is cleaned up after insertion. Keyboard-pasted PNG/WebM
SHA256 hashes match fixtures exactly.
- Native clipboard payloads are controlled fixtures because terminal
Win32 clipboard access is denied (error 5); physical OS clipboard file
seeding remains unverified.

The first CI run's full ESLint process was killed with exit 137.

agentHost: anchor Copilot customizations to each chat's own folders (#341694)

* agentHost: anchor Copilot customization discovery to each chat's own folders

A Copilot peer chat in a multi-folder session discovered the session's
customizations: the first folder's only (multi-root off) or the union of
all folders (multi-root on), instead of those of the folder it works in.

A chat's customization anchors are now its own effective working
directories (its first, plus its others when multi-root is enabled).
Discovery moves out of the session's plugin controller into refcounted
per-anchor-set `CustomizationAnchor`s: chats in the same folder share one,
a set is never discovered twice, and it is released with the last chat
using it and on session finalize. The session's ActiveClient keeps the
client tool set and client plugins, so client updates still reach every
chat. The published view (`SessionState.customizations`) stays the
default chat's and now follows a chat-only move of the default chat;
`copilot.sharedCustomizationDirectories` is still written for older
builds but no longer read for anchoring. MCP runtime-state publishing is
unchanged.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: test per-chat Copilot customization anchors

Pins each rule of the per-chat anchoring fix:
- a peer in a session's second folder gets that folder's agents,
  instructions and workspace MCP servers, not the first folder's
  (multi-root off) nor the union (multi-root on); its other folders only
  when multi-root is on; the default chat and the published view are
  unchanged;
- the default chat follows a chat-only move immediately and on relaunch,
  sharing a peer's discovery there, while `copilot.sharedCustomizationDirectories`
  is still written for older builds;
- the published view stays the default chat's when a peer starts first
  after a restart;
- chats in the same folder share one discovery;
- client tool updates reach every chat;
- a folder's discovery is released with its last chat and every
  discovery with the session;
- a peer's folder-only MCP server still appears in the session list
  (MCP runtime-state publishing unchanged);
- host session settings anchor to the default chat's own folders.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: resolve a Copilot peer's selected agent from the session's picker list

Agent pickers list the session's published customizations, which are the
default chat's (Agents window `agentHostAgentPicker` via the provider's
`getCustomAgents`, editor `AgentHostCustomizationService.getCustomAgents`,
both reading `SessionState.customizations`). With per-chat anchors a peer
in another folder could select a listed agent its own folder does not
discover, and it would not resolve.

When a chat's selected custom agent is not in its own anchor set's
snapshot, that one agent is taken from the published (default chat's)
anchor set at create, materialize, resume and send. Instructions and
skills stay the chat's own folder's.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: keep publishing the default chat's customizations after its anchor moves

Review findings on the per-chat anchors:
- The published view only republished discovery changes of the anchor
  set it had last read, so after a reanchor (worktree materialization,
  default-chat resume, a chat-only move) changes in the new folder were
  dropped until something re-read the view. Changes are now matched by
  the anchor set's key. A chat-only move of the default chat, which no
  host operation republishes, publishes the new view once it settles.
- A read overlapping session teardown could throw on the disposed
  published reference, or create discovery that nothing disposes. A
  disposed controller or anchor set now discovers nothing.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: expect the default chat's moved folder to be discovered at the move

A chat-only move of the default chat now publishes the new folder's
customizations once they settle, so that folder is discovered during
the move and the next send shares it instead of discovering it.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: key Copilot customization anchor sets by their folders' real paths

The same folder reached through different spellings (a symlink such as
`/tmp` and `/private/tmp` on macOS, or a different case where paths
ignore case) was keyed as two anchor sets, so it was discovered twice.
Anchor-set keys are now the comparison keys of the folders' real paths,
resolved before a chat acquires its set. Only the key changes: chats
keep running in, and anchor sets keep discovering, the folders they were
given.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: address review on per-chat Copilot customization anchors

- Keep the compatibility roots older builds discover from across repeated
  chat-only moves of the default chat: the roots saved by the first move
  are preserved instead of being replaced by the intermediate folder.
- Re-key live anchor sets once their folders' real paths resolve, so a
  set acquired under its spelling (e.g. by a client customization sync
  publishing before a chat launches through a symlink) is shared rather
  than discovered again.
- Create the test's directory link as a junction on Windows, where
  directory symlinks need extra privileges.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: drain session state before disposing services in the subagent restore test

The test disposed each AgentService and closed the database without the
session state drain that shutdown() performs. When the 250ms mirror flush
timer fired before the dispose (as on slower Windows runners), the flush's
transaction ran into the closed database, its rollback failed too, and the
store logged "AggregateError: Failed to mark the session state mirrored",
failing the test's errors assertion.

Drain each service's session state store before disposing it, and hold the
timer-driven flush in flight across the first dispose so the race is
reproduced deterministically.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: wait for the passive toggle's publish instead of a tick budget

"a read/archive toggle on an un-loaded session persists and publishes
without restoring it" waited at most 20 zero-delay ticks for the summary
notification. The toggle publishes only after loading the session's central
state from SQLite, which on a loaded runner (macOS Electron-Unit) takes
longer, so the test read neither the persisted value nor the published
status.

Wait for the notification itself (bounded), then drain session state and
catalog writes before reading, and slow the central state read in the test so
a tick-budget wait fails deterministically.

Fix lost race leaving a signed-out user on an Available marketplace (#331800)

* Fix sign-out race in workbench extension gallery manifest service

A sign-out during an in-flight manifest fetch could leave a signed-out
user looking at an Available marketplace. Two defects combined to the
same end state:

1. Dropped event: the onDidChangeDefaultAccount listener was registered
   after the initial await, so a sign-out during the startup fetch fired
   with nothing listening. The fetch then completed and published
   Available, and the currentStatus !== Available guard meant nothing
   re-fetched to correct it.
2. Lost race: even once the listener was registered, there was no
   supersession. A sign-out mid-fetch set RequiresSignIn, then the stale
   fetch resolved and published Available.

Register the account listener before the initial await, and add a
cancellation generation (beginResolution) so a superseded run cannot
publish. Both are required: moving the listener alone still loses the
race, and cancellation alone still drops the startup event.

could resolve with null while the replacement fetch was still pending. The
constructor publishes that value once to the shared-process and remote

settles while the second is pending) and await the sign-out test promise

agentHost: split the provider seam by chat owner (Block 3c) (#341734)

* agentHost: give providers a live reference to a chat's owner (Block 3c)

Chat contexts now carry `owner`, a reference that resolves the session owning
the chat from the chat registry each time it is read, alongside the existing
configurationResource. The registry can reassign a chat's owner internally
(live registry only, nothing persisted) and reports the change, so later
blocks can move chats while they run. Adds resolveSessionBackedStorage, which
tells a chat stored in its session's database from one stored under its own
resource, from the recorded storage.

No behaviour change: nothing reads `owner` yet and nothing reassigns owners.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: hand providers host-built chat contexts from conversions and slash completions (Block 3c)

The workspace conversion service passed a bare session URI as the chat
context to getChatCustomizations, setWorkingDirectory, releaseChat and
disposeChat, and built one context by hand; slash completions built the
default chat's context by hand with its session as storage. Both now use the
host's context builder, so providers see the chat's recorded storage and its
live owner.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: resolve retained terminal links through their chat (Block 3c)

A retained (non-PTY) terminal link embeds the session and storage it was
written under. Opening one restored that embedded session, refused unless the
chat's owner still matched it, and read the output from the embedded storage;
subscription routing also used the embedded session. That inferred the owner
from the link.

Links now resolve through the chat they name: its current owner (restored if
needed, subagent chats through their recorded owner) and its recorded
storage, and the reported claim names the current owner. Subscriptions track
terminal links per chat, so routing follows owner changes. The link format is
unchanged: new builds keep writing the session and storage for older builds
and no longer read them.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: key turn checkpoints by chat and detect concurrent turns per repository (Block 3c)

A turn's start checkpoint was kept under the session that owned its chat, so
a turn whose chat changes owner before it ends would find no start and lose
its Git turn diff. Start records are now keyed by chat and turn and carry the
session the turn started under; the end writes under that session's baseline
and ref namespace.

Concurrent-turn detection moves from "another turn of the same session" to
"another turn in the same repository", whichever session owns it: after
moves, chats of different sessions can share a working tree. Turns of one
session in different repositories now keep their Git checkpoints; turns of
different sessions in one repository now fall back to tracked edits, as
concurrent turns of one session already did.

Side effects' owners recorded for teardown follow a chat's owner changes.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: open chats' databases by their recorded storage (Block 3c)

Several host paths opened a chat's database through its chat URI, or a
session's default chat's through the session: the changeset service's
tracked-edit databases (peer turn sources, the session's union of peer
databases, chat Session Changes), the rollback of a failed chat creation,
the v2 catalog registration's default-chat storage fallback, and Mission
Control's replication cursors. They now use the storage recorded for the
chat. The changeset service keeps a turn's identity (folders, checkpoints)
separate from the database it reads, and file-edit content URIs embed the
database's storage.

No change for existing chats: their recorded storage is what the URI-derived
rule gave. It matters once a chat stores somewhere other than its URI (a
session's default chat moved under another session).

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: write older-build copies only for chats stored at their chat URI (Block 3c)

Older builds read a peer's own data from a database at its chat URI. The
copies written for them (a normalized peer's working directories, and the
session state store's mirrors into chat databases) now go only to chats whose
recorded storage is that URI; a chat stored elsewhere, which older builds do
not know as a peer, gets none instead of a stray empty database.

Legacy-catalog sessions record no storage, so their chats' storage is still
the URI-derived rule; those reads and writes now go through one named helper,

* agentHost: persist a chat's own config in its own database (Block 3b)

The values a chat sets for itself are stored under

* agentHost: resolve sandbox enablement per chat (Block 3b)

A chat's sandbox selection is its own value over the session's, within the
session's policy floor. The sandbox APIs take the chat and its session:

- The applied enablement is recorded per chat in the session's
  `vscode.sandboxState` metadata (`chats[chat]`), read through a typed,
  validating reader. The session-level fields keep describing the default
  chat for older clients.
- A policy that requires sandboxing turns a chat's own `off` back on, like
  the session's.
- A rejected change rolls back where the selection was set (the chat's own
  values or the session's), unless a newer selection superseded it.
- Copilot's SDK sandbox, its terminal sandbox engine and its browser tool
  restrictions apply the chat's selection; a session opt-out from a
  permission request changes that chat only.

`getChatConfigValues` returns the same object while its inputs are unchanged,
which keeps the superseded-request check based on identity.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: elevate Agent Merge's autonomous config per owning chat (Block 3b)

folder; the per-chat bookkeeping (`agentMerge.chatInjectedConfiguration`,

waits for an active turn.

Properties no chat may set keep the session-wide elevation and its
bookkeeping, which also rolls back session-wide elevation an older build
applied. Folder enablement and lifecycle stay per (session, folder).

A fork or side chat copies its source chat's own values without the
elevation.

Private Marketplace extension blocking: add gallery and install enforcement (#333859)

* Surface extensions blocked by the marketplace

The marketplace previously omitted extensions it would not serve, so a
user searching for one saw an empty result and no reason for it. It now
returns the record carrying a `blocked` flag instead, and this reads
that flag and explains the block rather than letting the extension
disappear.

The flag comes at two granularities -- a whole extension, or a single
version while the others remain available -- and both are read. A
blocked version is skipped when selecting one to acquire, so selection
falls through to a permitted version, in display paths as well as
install paths: a version pinned out by policy is usually the newest,
and showing it would strand an extension whose earlier versions are
perfectly usable. The two granularities are not distinguished in the
result, because a block only reaches a user once no version is
permitted, and at that point the extension is unavailable to them
whichever granularity produced it.

Blocked extensions are still returned by the gallery, so enforcement
lives at the decision points -- canInstall, auto-update, and the
extensionDisallowInstall context key -- rather than by filtering them
out of results. The block takes precedence over deprecation, and the
message distinguishes an organization policy decision from a
marketplace statement, since conflating the two either alarms users
about a routine policy decision or understates a marketplace finding.

Report the reason canInstall determined when refusing an install, rather
than discarding it for a fixed platform-incompatibility message. That
message was already wrong for an allow list denial, and adding a second
cause to the same path would have made a blocked extension claim it was
unavailable for the machine's platform, sending the user to look for one
that could run it. The paths reaching this are the ones with no other
signal: settings sync, the command line, and the URI handler.

Only the flag and the origin are read. The contract also defines a
reason, none of whose values the registry populates today: allow-list
denials are the only blocks issued, and they carry origin policy. Origin
is kept rather than collapsed to a boolean because attributing a
marketplace block to the user's own organization would be misleading.
Absent, unrecognized, and wrong-typed values degrade to the marketplace
wording rather than failing the parse, which would have taken down the
whole query rather than the one extension.
